raw_response.country: Multiple African countries (regional overview of Africa and sub-Saharan Africa)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household and community access to water services (piped network connections, standpipes/kiosks, tankers, vendors, resellers, and improved drinking water) in African cities, focusing on low-income areas (LIA) and informal settlements (IS).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: This paper passes the broad plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain = yes) because it narratively discusses institutional and governance dimensions of water sector financing (public vs. private sector participation/PPPs, Structural Adjustment fiscal austerity, political sensitivity to tariff increases, and colonial urban planning legacies), even though overall full-text eligibility still fails on Criteria 3 and 5. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, Criterion 2 is NOT met (narrow = no): the paper focuses on macro-level capital infrastructure investment deficits, foreign direct investment flows, and demographic growth as unanalysed macro-governance/financing background rather than analysing a rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory rules) directly governing household service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Narrative policy and status overview with no empirical research method, no analytical study design, and no systematic synthesis methodology. Tables 1-7 merely reproduce or recalculate aggregate descriptive statistics from secondary international reports and databases (UN-HABITAT 2013, Gleick et al. 2011, Keener et al. 2010, and IBNET), supplemented by a single uncontextualised illustrative quote from an unpublished 2007 interview CD without reported sampling or methods. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports secondary descriptive statistics on urban access to improved drinking water (Table 5) and household modes of accessing water across 23 African cities, including household piped connections, standpipes/kiosks, tankers, household resellers, and water vendors (Table 6).
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design and does not define or test an empirical relationship between a specific legal/administrative exposure and a household or community access outcome; units in reproduced tables shift across regions, countries, cities, and utilities for descriptive illustration only.

evidence_quotes.quote: The main purpose of this article is to discuss the status of access to water services in the poorer parts of African cities. The article illustrates that low-capital investments in water services infrastructure, high population growth in LIA and IS areas, low political priority given to water services, as well as the failure to restructure the colonial urban planning and management patterns, have contributed to the challenges that many poor urban dwellers in African cities are facing today.
Using data from various sources, this article illustrates the growing challenge posed by inadequate water services infrastructure in the midst of the rapidly growing urban population.
This investment pattern has serious implications for the existing water services infrastructure funding gap in Africa, in the context of the rapidly growing urban population.

From the discussion above, it is apparent that one of the biggest challenges for water services in most African countries and cities is the low funding dedicated to water infrastructure maintenance and development.
Table 6 shows different modes of accessing water for selected major cities in Africa, together with the proportion of people living in LIA and IS.

raw_response.exposure: Macro-level water infrastructure capital funding deficits, public vs. private investment trends, and rapid urban population growth (no specific rule-type legal or administrative mechanism empirically analysed)
raw_response.outcome: Secondary descriptive rates of urban access to improved drinking water, household modes of accessing water (individual connection, standpipe/kiosk, water tanker, household resellers, water vendors), and utility non-revenue water (%)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban populations, especially residents in low-income areas (LIA) and informal settlements (IS), across African countries and 23 selected cities (secondary aggregate figures from UN-HABITAT, Gleick et al., Keener et al., and IBNET; no primary sample)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude as E05 (No empirical evidence). Chitonge (2014) is a macro-level narrative policy and sector status overview of urban water services and infrastructure financing gaps across African cities. It contains no empirical methodology, no primary data collection design (aside from one brief uncontextualised quote from an unpublished 2007 CD), and no systematic synthesis protocol, relying instead on descriptive summary tables compiled from UN-HABITAT, World Bank (Keener et al.), Gleick et al., and IBNET reports. It also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it examines macro-level capital investment shortfalls, demographic pressure, and broad private-sector investment avoidance rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household water access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded due to the absence of an empirical study design or empirical analysis (Criteria 3 and 5).
raw_response.study_design: Narrative policy and sector overview compiling secondary descriptive statistics
